cross_response_observations: Analysis of 24 candidate responses reveals systematic failure patterns in worst-case reasoning for the sequence-envelope puzzle. The canonical answer of 15 inspections (1 for initial 'Mixed' identification + 14 to prove purity against 7/13 mixed envelope) was correctly identified by only 3 responses (C, K, W). The most common error (appearing in responses A, D, I, Q, S, U) was the 'fatal wrong claim' that remaining envelopes are 'forced by elimination' or 'uniquely determined' after minimal inspections, ignoring that a single observation cannot distinguish pure from mixed envelopes. Many responses (B, F, H, J, L, M, V) failed with 'invalid one-draw inference', assuming 1-4 inspections suffice when 15 are needed. Information-theoretic approaches (Response O) and minority-majority miscounts (P, T claiming 8-9 instead of 15) show misunderstanding of the adversarial worst-case where mixed envelopes reveal majority type for first 13 draws. The 'non-terminating' response X uniquely denies a finite solution exists. Two responses (E, N) exhibited 'contradictory final answer' by oscillating among incompatible counts without coherent commitment. Only responses C, K, and W correctly applied the 7/13 structure to derive 14+1=15.
